CausalChain: SF3B2 upregulation (+ synergy with SF3B1/SF3B4) -> Altered splicing of DNA repair genes (TP53, RAD51) -> Impaired DNA repair and permissive chromatin environment -> Enhanced viral DNA integration -> Genomic instability -> Activation of metastasis and angiogenesis -> Poor liver neoplasm prognosis
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that in a subset of liver neoplasms, overexpression of SF3B2, together with co-dysregulated splicing factors (e.g., SF3B1 and SF3B4), leads to the production of aberrant splice variants of critical DNA repair regulators such as TP53 and RAD51. This event impairs the cellular DNA repair machinery and creates a permissive environment for viral DNA integration. The integration events further exacerbate genomic instability, which in turn triggers oncogenic pathways—specifically those involved in metastasis and angiogenesis—resulting in worsened clinical outcomes. To test this hypothesis, we will utilize high-throughput RNA sequencing (including single-cell RNA-seq), CRISPR interference screens, and long-read sequencing to map viral integration sites. These technologies will facilitate a detailed mechanistic exploration of how SF3B2-mediated splicing alterations drive liver tumor progression, thereby bridging critical gaps between splicing dysregulation, viral integration, and oncogenesis.
Abstract: In liver neoplasms, we hypothesize that elevated expression of the splicing factor SF3B2, acting in concert with other splicing modulators such as SF3B1 and SF3B4, drives a distinct splicing signature in key DNA repair genes including TP53 and RAD51. This aberrant splicing network compromises DNA repair fidelity and creates a cellular context that favors the integration of viral DNA into the host genome, thereby promoting genomic instability. The resultant instability further activates oncogenic pathways, particularly those governing metastasis and angiogenesis, culminating in a poorer clinical prognosis. Leveraging contemporary technologies such as high-resolution RNA sequencing, CRISPR-based functional genomics, and long-read sequencing approaches for precise mapping of viral integration sites, our integrative framework aims to delineate the mechanistic interplay of these molecular events and validate their role in liver cancer progression.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that SF3B2 upregulation leads to aberrant splicing of TP53 and RAD51, promoting viral DNA integration, genomic instability, and ultimately a poor prognosis in liver neoplasms. The revised hypothesis retains this causal framework but refines it by incorporating evidence that other splicing factors (e.g., SF3B1 and SF3B4) also contribute to dysregulated splicing in liver cancer. It further enhances practical implementability by proposing the use of state-of-the-art genomic and transcriptomic tools (e.g., CRISPR screens, single-cell RNA-seq, and long-read sequencing) to experimentally validate each step of the causal chain. This integrated approach not only preserves the novelty of linking splicing dysregulation to viral integration but also offers concrete methodologies to dissect the mechanistic interplay of these pathways in liver cancer progression.
